items.prompt: Why does skin need several different types of touch receptor rather than just one?

options.label: Because each type is tuned to a different kind of pressure or movement
options.feedback: A light brush, a steady press and a fast vibration are physically different events, each answered best by its own receptor.

options.label: So one type can rest while another works
options.feedback: Several types are often active in the same patch of skin at once; they don't take turns resting.

options.label: So the skin can send the same signal from more places
options.feedback: What varies between receptor types is what they detect, not simply how many copies of one signal get sent.

options.label: To make the skin thicker for protection
options.feedback: Skin thickness comes from its layered structure, not from how many kinds of receptor sit within it.

items.ok_line: One receptor built to answer one kind of touch well tends to answer the others poorly.
items.ko_title: Not rest, not repetition, not thickness
items.ko_line: A light brush and a steady press are genuinely different physical events — think about what that demands.
items.exp_text: A light brush, a steady press, a fast vibration and a stretch of the skin are physically different events, and a single receptor built to answer one of those questions well tends to answer the others poorly. So skin carries several distinct receptor types side by side, each built with a different shape and depth so that it picks out one particular kind of touch while staying fairly quiet for the others.

items.prompt: Why do you stop noticing the feeling of clothes on your skin a few minutes after getting dressed?

options.label: The clothes press less hard once they warm up
options.feedback: Clothing doesn't loosen or press more gently just from warming to body temperature; the pressure on the skin stays much the same.

options.label: The skin becomes numb from lack of air
options.feedback: Skin under clothing gets plenty of air exchange through the fabric; numbness from suffocation isn't what's happening.

options.label: The receptors under constant, unchanging pressure reduce their signalling
options.feedback: Many touch receptors respond strongly at first, then quickly reduce how often they fire under a steady, unchanging pressure.

options.label: The nerves carrying the signal get physically tired and stop working
options.feedback: Those same nerves respond instantly and fully the moment something changes, like the fabric shifting, so they haven't stopped working.

items.ok_title: A signal that quiets, not a nerve that quits
items.ok_line: The receptors are still there and still working — they've just stopped reporting something unchanging.
items.ko_title: Not warmth, not numbness, not exhaustion
items.ko_line: Move your arm and the clothes are noticed again instantly — so nothing has actually stopped working.
items.exp_title: A signal that fades when nothing is new
items.exp_text: Many touch receptors respond strongly the instant a pressure begins, then quickly reduce how often they fire if that same pressure just sits there unchanged. Because the waistband or collar keeps pressing at a steady, unvarying level once it's on, the signal reporting it dies down and awareness of it drops away, at least until you move and the pressure changes again.

items.prompt: Why can your fingertip feel fine detail, like the grain of paper, that the skin on your back can't detect at all?

options.label: The back has thicker skin that blocks the sensation
options.feedback: The back's skin isn't so much thicker that it would block fine detail; what differs is how receptors are arranged underneath.

options.label: The fingertip has a special type of receptor the back lacks entirely
options.feedback: The same general types of receptor are present in both places; it's how tightly they're spaced that differs.

options.label: The back's nerves take longer to send their signal
options.feedback: Signal speed along the nerve doesn't change what fine detail an area can resolve.

options.label: The fingertip's receptors are packed much more closely together
options.feedback: Closely packed receptors let two nearby points land on separate receptors instead of blurring into one.

items.ok_title: Detail is a matter of spacing
items.ok_line: It isn't a special receptor or thicker skin — it's how tightly the receptors sit together.
items.ko_title: Not thickness, not a special type, not speed
items.ko_line: The same kinds of receptor exist in both places — what changes is how densely they're arranged.
items.exp_title: Detail depends on spacing, not just presence
items.exp_text: Telling two nearby points apart depends on having two separate receptors close enough together that each point lands on its own one, rather than both landing on the same receptor and blurring into a single sensation. Receptors on the fingertip sit much closer together than receptors on the back do, so the fingertip can resolve fine texture that would blur into one vague pressure anywhere the receptors are spaced further apart.

items.prompt: How does a nerve ending wrapped around the base of a hair let you feel something brushing against skin you can't even see touched?

options.label: The hair itself has no role; the skin beneath is what responds
options.feedback: Skin with the hair plucked out becomes noticeably less sensitive to a light brush in that spot, which shows the hair itself is doing real work.

options.label: The hair acts like a lever, and even a slight bend of it moves the nerve ending wrapped around its base
options.feedback: A small movement at the tip of the hair becomes a much bigger tug at the buried base, where the nerve ending sits.

options.label: The hair changes colour when touched, which the skin detects
options.feedback: Nothing about a hair's colour changes from being brushed, and skin has no way to detect colour regardless.

options.label: The hair vibrates and creates a sound the skin hears
options.feedback: Skin has no way to hear anything; the sensation here is entirely a matter of mechanical bending, not sound.

items.ok_title: A lever, not a passive strand
items.ok_line: The hair itself is doing mechanical work before the nerve ever fires.
items.ko_line: Pluck the hair out and sensitivity in that spot actually drops — so it must be contributing something.
items.exp_title: A lever that turns a light touch into a bigger tug
items.exp_text: A hair sticking up out of the skin acts like a small lever: an object brushing against its tip only has to move the hair a little, but that small movement at the tip becomes a much bigger tug at the buried base. A nerve ending wrapped tightly around that base picks up the tug and fires, which is why even a faint stir of air moving a single hair can be felt clearly.

items.prompt: Are the receptors that detect pain the same ones that detect ordinary touch, just responding more strongly?

options.label: No, pain is detected by a separate set of free nerve endings tuned to potential damage
options.feedback: These free nerve endings stay quiet under gentle contact and fire once a stimulus risks damaging tissue.

options.label: Yes, any touch receptor fires as pain once the pressure is strong enough
options.feedback: Ordinary touch receptors actually stop increasing their signal well before a pressure becomes damaging.

options.label: Yes, but only in the fingertips
options.feedback: The distinction between pain receptors and touch receptors holds true across the whole body, not just in one area.

options.label: No, pain is detected by the same receptors that sense temperature
options.feedback: Temperature receptors and pain receptors are two more separate sets again; a burn is reported by both together, but neither substitutes for the other.

items.ok_title: A separate sensor, for a separate purpose
items.ok_line: Pain isn't ordinary touch turned up loud — it's its own dedicated warning system.
items.ko_title: Not the same receptor, and not the fingertips only
items.ko_line: Ordinary touch receptors actually saturate before things get dangerous — something else has to take over.
items.exp_title: A different sensor built for a different job
items.exp_text: Ordinary touch receptors are built to report gentle contact and saturate quickly, giving little extra signal once a pressure moves well past a light touch. Free nerve endings scattered through the skin serve as the pain sensor instead, staying quiet under gentle contact and firing specifically once a pressure, temperature or chemical crosses into a range that risks damaging tissue.

items.prompt: When you touch something icy cold, is that coldness detected by the same receptors that detect pressure?

options.label: Yes, pressure receptors simply fire faster when something is cold
options.feedback: Pressure receptors respond to how hard and how fast something presses, not to temperature.

options.label: Yes, because cold objects always press harder
options.feedback: An ice cube resting gently on skin presses no harder than a warm object of the same weight.

options.label: No, separate receptors respond specifically to changes in temperature
options.feedback: Cooling or warming a patch of skin changes how its dedicated temperature receptors fire, apart from any pressure signal.

options.label: No, temperature is only sensed by the tongue and lips
options.feedback: Skin all over the body carries its own temperature receptors, which is how you can feel a cold doorknob with your hand.

items.ok_title: Two different questions, two different sensors
items.ok_line: Pressure and temperature are answered by receptors that don't overlap.
items.ko_title: Not extra pressure, and not the mouth alone
items.ko_line: A gentle, light-weight ice cube still feels distinctly cold — so pressure alone can't be the explanation.
items.exp_title: One sensor for pressure, another for heat
items.exp_text: Pressure and temperature are two entirely different physical events at the skin's surface, and each is picked up by its own dedicated receptor rather than one receptor doing double duty. Cooling or warming a patch of skin changes how the temperature receptors there fire, entirely apart from whatever the pressure receptors in that same patch happen to be reporting.

items.prompt: Is an itch simply a very mild version of pain, using the same signal?

options.label: Yes, itch and pain are identical signals at different strengths
options.feedback: Scratching, itself a form of mild pain, actually relieves an itch — a strange result if the two were simply the same signal turned down.

options.label: Yes, itch is just pain detected in hairier skin
options.feedback: Itch happens just as readily on hairless skin, like the palm, so hair has nothing to do with it.

options.label: No, itch is detected by the same receptors as taste
options.feedback: Taste receptors sit in the mouth and have no connection at all to sensations felt on the skin.

options.label: No, itch travels along its own distinct set of nerve fibres
options.feedback: Certain nerve fibres respond specifically to itch-triggering substances and stay silent to what triggers pain.

items.ok_title: Its own signal, not pain turned down
items.ok_line: Itch runs on a pathway separate enough that a scratch can interrupt it without touching pain at all.
items.ko_title: Not the same signal, and not about hair or taste
items.ko_line: A mild pain like a scratch shouldn't relieve another mild pain — unless the two aren't the same signal at all.
items.exp_title: Its own signal, not pain turned down low
items.exp_text: For a long time itch was assumed to be a weak form of pain, but certain nerve fibres respond specifically to itch-triggering substances and stay silent to the kind of stimulation that triggers pain. Because that pathway runs separately from the one carrying pain, scratching can interrupt the itch signal without needing to override any pain signal at all, which is why a scratch brings such quick relief.

items.prompt: How can your fingertip tell that a phone in your pocket is buzzing, before you even see or hear it?

options.label: Ordinary touch receptors are triggered by any object nearby
options.feedback: A phone sitting still in a pocket, not vibrating, barely registers at all; it's the rapid vibration specifically that gets noticed.

options.label: A receptor type deep in the skin responds specifically to fast, repeated pressure changes
options.feedback: This receptor picks up rapid, rhythmic pressure while staying largely quiet under a slow, steady one.

options.label: The warmth of the phone's battery is what's actually detected
options.feedback: Warmth is picked up by temperature receptors and takes much longer to build up than the near-instant sense that something is buzzing.

options.label: Sound from the phone travels through clothing to the ear
options.feedback: A phone can be felt buzzing through a pocket even in a loud room where its sound can't be heard at all.

items.ok_line: It isn't warmth, sound, or mere presence — it's a receptor built specifically for rapid, repeating pressure.
items.ko_line: A silent, buzzing phone is still felt clearly, and a warm, still one isn't — so what's the actual trigger?
items.exp_title: A receptor built to ring with rapid pressure
items.exp_text: A rapidly repeating pattern of tiny pressure changes, like a buzzing phone, is a different physical event from a single steady push, and skin carries a receptor type built specifically to catch that repetition. Layered like an onion around a nerve ending, this receptor picks up fast, rhythmic pressure while staying largely quiet under a slow, steady one, letting a pocketed phone's buzz stand out clearly from the constant pressure of the fabric around it.

items.prompt: Why does your hand jerk away from a hot stove before you consciously feel any pain?

options.label: The signal triggers muscles directly through the spinal cord, without waiting for a longer route
options.feedback: A pain signal can be switched right at the spinal cord onto a nerve heading back to the arm's muscles, triggering the pull-away early.

options.label: Pain travels faster than any other type of signal in the body
options.feedback: The withdrawal happens quickly not because the pain signal is unusually fast, but because of a shortcut it takes on the way.

options.label: The hand pulls away out of habit, from past experience with heat
options.feedback: The very first time a person ever touches something hot, before any such experience exists, the hand still jerks away just as fast.

options.label: Heat itself makes the muscles contract, with no nerve signal involved
options.feedback: A hand with its nerves numbed by anaesthetic won't pull away from heat at all, which shows a nerve signal is doing the work.

items.ok_line: The signal isn't faster — it just skips the longer trip before triggering the muscle.
items.ko_title: Not habit, and not muscle acting alone
items.ko_line: A first-ever touch to something hot still produces the same instant pull-away, with no experience behind it.
items.exp_title: A shortcut that skips the longer trip
items.exp_text: A pain signal travelling up the arm can be switched, right there at the spinal cord, directly onto a nerve heading back out to the arm's muscles, triggering the pull-away before the signal has even finished its longer trip further up. Because the muscle contraction is set off by that short local loop, the hand is already moving away from the stove by the time the fuller signal registers as felt pain.

items.prompt: How does your hand know to grip a slippery glass more tightly the instant it starts to slide, often before you notice it slipping?

options.label: Muscles in the hand contract automatically whenever they get tired
options.feedback: Tiredness in the hand's muscles has nothing to do with the timing here; the tightening happens the instant slipping starts.

options.label: The eyes detect the glass moving and send a warning signal
options.feedback: The grip tightens just as fast with the eyes closed, so this isn't something that depends on seeing the glass move.

options.label: Receptors in the fingertip skin detect the tiny stretch and vibration of the surface starting to slide and trigger a quick grip response
options.feedback: The skin stretches and shudders in a distinctive way the instant an object begins to slip, and receptors tuned to that pattern catch it early.

options.label: Sweat on the fingers automatically increases grip through stickiness
options.feedback: Sweat changes slowly over time and isn't released in the instant something starts to slip.

items.ok_title: Skin that catches the first hint
items.ok_line: The grip tightens because the skin itself detects the earliest sign of a slide.
items.ko_title: Not the eyes, not sweat, not fatigue
items.ko_line: This works with the eyes closed and happens far too fast for sweat or tiredness to explain.
items.exp_title: Skin that reports the first hint of a slide
items.exp_text: The moment an object grasped in the hand begins to slip, the skin gripping it stretches and shudders in a distinctive way, different from the steady pattern of a secure hold. Receptors tuned to exactly that kind of tiny stretch and vibration catch the change and trigger a fast increase in grip force through the same short spinal loop used for pulling away from pain, tightening the hold before the object has slipped far enough to notice.
